chapterTitle: The King's Design — Marriage, Children, and the Cost of the Kingdom
themeTitle: "What God Has Joined Together, Let No Man Separate"

scripture.text: When Jesus had finished these words, he departed from Galilee, and came into the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan.
scripture.understanding: The fourth of Matthew's five great discourses (the community-and-forgiveness teaching of chapter 18) is now complete — you can hear the signature refrain, "When Jesus had finished these words." The King now turns his face south, out of Galilee toward Judea and Jerusalem, where the cross is waiting.

scripture.text: Great multitudes followed him, and he healed them there.
scripture.understanding: Even on the road to His own suffering, the King's compassion does not stop. He heals as He goes. The Kingdom does not arrive as mere doctrine; it arrives as mercy touching broken bodies.

scripture.text: Pharisees came to him, testing him, and saying, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?”
scripture.understanding: This is not an honest question — it is a trap. The rabbis were split: the school of Shammai allowed divorce only for immorality, the school of Hillel for "any reason" (even a burned meal). They want to catch Jesus siding against one camp and losing the crowd, and perhaps to snare Him against Herod as they had John the Baptist.

scripture.text: He answered, “Haven’t you read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female,
scripture.understanding: Jesus refuses their rabbinic loophole and goes over their heads to Genesis. "Haven't you read?" — the sharpest rebuke you can give a Bible scholar. He anchors the whole question of marriage not in Moses' concession but in the Creator's original act.

scripture.text: and said, ‘For this cause a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall be joined to his wife; and the two shall become one flesh?’
scripture.understanding: Quoting Genesis 2:24, Jesus defines marriage as a leaving, a cleaving, and a becoming. Two whole persons are fused into a single new reality — "one flesh" — a bond of body, soul, and covenant.

scripture.text: So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.”
scripture.understanding: Here is the thunderclap of the chapter. Marriage is not a human contract you may cancel; it is a divine welding. God Himself is the one who joins — so the severing is not a private choice but a defiance of God's own handiwork.

scripture.text: They asked him, “Why then did Moses command us to give her a bill of divorce, and divorce her?”
scripture.understanding: The Pharisees think they have their counter: doesn't Deuteronomy 24 command divorce? Notice their slippery word — Moses "commanded." They have upgraded a reluctant permission into a divine order.

scripture.text: He said to them, “Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it has not been so.
scripture.understanding: Jesus corrects them precisely: Moses did not command — he allowed. And he allowed it as a concession to human sin, a legal fence to protect discarded women in a hard-hearted culture. God's ideal never changed; "from the beginning it has not been so."

scripture.text: I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery; and he who marries her when she is divorced commits adultery.”
scripture.understanding: With "I tell you," the King speaks with an authority above Moses. He restores the marriage bond to its original weight: to shatter a covenant and marry another is adultery. The single stated exception is sexual immorality (Greek porneia), which itself has already ruptured the one-flesh union.

scripture.text: His disciples said to him, “If this is the case of the man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.”
scripture.understanding: The disciples are stunned. If marriage is this permanent, this binding, this beyond escape — then perhaps it is safer never to marry at all. Their reaction reveals how low the culture's view of marriage had sunk.

scripture.text: But he said to them, “Not all men can receive this saying, but those to whom it is given.
scripture.understanding: Jesus does not scold their shock; He acknowledges the weight. The capacity to live singleness (or this high view of marriage) as a gift is itself something God grants. Not everyone is given the same road.

scripture.text: For there are eunuchs who were born that way from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the Kingdom of Heaven’s sake. He who is able to receive it, let him receive it.”
scripture.understanding: Jesus honors voluntary singleness for God's Kingdom as a genuine, holy calling — a life laid down for the King rather than a marriage. "Eunuch" here is figurative for the celibate; some renounce marriage to give themselves wholly to the Kingdom. He does not command it; He commends it to those able to receive it.

scripture.text: Then little children were brought to him, that he should lay his hands on them and pray; and the disciples rebuked them.
scripture.understanding: From marriage the scene flows naturally to its fruit — children. Parents bring their little ones for the Rabbi's blessing, but the disciples, guarding the King's time, treat the children as an interruption. They have not yet understood who belongs in this Kingdom.

scripture.text: But Jesus said, “Allow the little children, and don’t forbid them to come to me; for the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to ones like these.”
scripture.understanding: The King overrules His own gatekeepers. The children are not a distraction from the Kingdom — they are a portrait of it. Small, dependent, empty-handed, receiving everything as gift: this is the posture of everyone who enters.

scripture.text: He laid his hands on them, and departed from there.
scripture.understanding: He does exactly what the parents asked. Unhurried, tender, personal — the hands that will soon be nailed to a cross rest gently on the heads of children. Then He moves on toward the next encounter.

scripture.text: Behold, one came to him and said, “Good teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?”
scripture.understanding: A striking contrast to the children: here comes a man who wants to earn. His whole question is built on doing — "what good thing shall I do?" — the exact opposite of the child who simply receives. He is sincere, but he is trying to buy what can only be given.

scripture.text: He said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, that is, God. But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments.”
scripture.understanding: Jesus presses the man's careless flattery: if only God is good, and you call Me good, do you know what you are saying? Then He meets the man on his own terms — you want to earn life by doing? Very well: keep the commandments, all of them, perfectly.

scripture.text: He said to him, “Which ones?” Jesus said, “‘You shall not murder.’ ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ ‘You shall not steal.’ ‘You shall not offer false testimony.’
scripture.understanding: The man asks "which ones?" as if some commandments could be skipped. Jesus lists the second table of the Law — the commands about loving your neighbor — the visible, measurable ones the man is confident he has kept.

scripture.text: ‘Honor your father and your mother.’ And, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’”
scripture.understanding: Jesus caps the list with the great summary: love your neighbor as yourself. This is the hook. If the man truly loved his neighbor as himself, he would gladly share his great wealth — and in a moment we will discover he cannot.

scripture.text: The young man said to him, “All these things I have observed from my youth. What do I still lack?”
scripture.understanding: His answer is honest and revealing. Outwardly he has kept the rules his whole life — yet his own conscience knows something is missing. "What do I still lack?" is the ache of a religious man who has done everything and still feels empty.

scripture.text: Jesus said to him, “If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.”
scripture.understanding: The King's scalpel finds the tumor. The command is tailor-made: the one thing this man cannot surrender is his wealth, so that is exactly what Jesus asks for. It is not a universal command to sell everything; it is the exposure of this man's true god — and an invitation to trade it for Christ Himself.

scripture.text: But when the young man heard the saying, he went away sad, for he was one who had great possessions.
scripture.understanding: The saddest verse in the chapter. He came running with a great question and walks away with a heavy heart. He did not reject Jesus in anger — he simply loved his possessions more. His riches did not belong to him; he belonged to them.

scripture.text: Jesus said to his disciples, “Most certainly I say to you, a rich man will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven with difficulty.
scripture.understanding: Jesus turns the moment into a lesson. Wealth is not neutral; it is spiritually heavy. Riches breed self-sufficiency, and self-sufficiency is the very opposite of the child's empty-handed dependence that enters the Kingdom.

scripture.text: Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through a needle’s eye, than for a rich man to enter into God’s Kingdom.”
scripture.understanding: The largest animal in Palestine and the smallest opening imaginable — Jesus paints a picture of sheer impossibility, and He means it. Left to himself, no rich man (indeed no man) can squeeze his way into the Kingdom by his own resources.

scripture.text: When the disciples heard it, they were exceedingly astonished, saying, “Who then can be saved?”
scripture.understanding: The disciples grasp the shock. In their world, wealth was assumed to be a sign of God's favor — if the blessed rich can't get in, what hope is there for anyone? Their question is exactly the one Jesus wants them to ask.

scripture.text: Looking at them, Jesus said, “With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
scripture.understanding: Here is the gospel in a single sentence. Salvation is humanly impossible — for the rich and the poor alike. But what no man can do for himself, God does. The camel cannot thread the needle; God threads it. Grace accomplishes what effort never could.

scripture.text: Then Peter answered, “Behold, we have left everything, and followed you. What then will we have?”
scripture.understanding: Peter, ever blunt, says out loud what the others are thinking. The rich man would not leave everything; we did. What is in it for us? It is a raw, honest question — and Jesus does not rebuke it. He answers it with staggering generosity.

scripture.text: Jesus said to them, “Most certainly I tell you that you who have followed me, in the regeneration when the Son of Man will sit on the throne of his glory, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
scripture.understanding: Jesus lifts Peter's eyes past the present cost to the coming renewal of all things — the "regeneration," when creation itself is made new and the King sits enthroned in glory. Those who followed Him in His humiliation will share in His reign.

scripture.text: Everyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name’s sake, will receive one hundred times, and will inherit eternal life.
scripture.understanding: The promise widens from the Twelve to "everyone." Whatever you surrender for Christ's name, you do not lose — you exchange it for a hundredfold return now (in family and provision within God's household) and, beyond all reckoning, eternal life. No one ever out-gives God.

scripture.text: But many will be last who are first; and first who are last.
scripture.understanding: The King ends with a warning wrapped in a promise. God's Kingdom overturns the world's rankings. The rich young ruler who seemed "first" walked away last; the disciples who left everything and seemed to have nothing will be first. Do not measure by earthly scoreboards.

visualMeditations.title: The Divine Welding
visualMeditations.image: Picture a blacksmith taking two separate bars of iron, heating them white-hot, and hammering them together on the anvil until they cool as a single bar. There is no longer a seam, no clean line where one ends and the other begins. To pull them apart now is not to separate two things — it is to rip a single thing in two, and iron tears with a scream.
visualMeditations.meaning: Jesus says the two "become one flesh" — a new, single reality forged by God Himself. This is why He says God has "joined them together": the welder is divine. Divorce is not the tidy dissolving of a partnership; it is the violent tearing of a body that God has made one. Understanding this changes how you treat your covenant — and how seriously heaven takes it.

visualMeditations.title: The Children at the Gate
visualMeditations.image: See the dusty road, the King surrounded by important men debating important things, and at the edge of the crowd a cluster of mothers with toddlers on their hips and children tugging their sleeves. The disciples wave them off — not now, not here, the Master is busy. And then the King's voice cuts through: "Allow them." The crowd parts. The small ones come. Grown hands lift them up to the hands that made them.
visualMeditations.meaning: The children own nothing, have earned nothing, and can offer nothing but themselves. That is precisely why the Kingdom belongs to "ones like these." The disciples thought greatness was the qualification; Jesus shows that dependency is. The gate of the Kingdom is low — you have to become small to walk through it.

visualMeditations.title: The Camel and the Needle
visualMeditations.image: Now hold two pictures side by side: the largest beast anyone in Judea had ever seen — a camel, loaded, humped, towering — and the tiniest hole anyone could imagine, the eye of a sewing needle held up to the light. Jesus deliberately jams them together. The camel cannot fold itself small enough. The eye cannot stretch wide enough. It is not hard; it is impossible.
visualMeditations.meaning: Jesus is not offering a technique for rich people to slim down and slip through. He is closing the door on human effort entirely. And it lands even harder when you realize the disciples' response — "who then can be saved?" The point is not that the rich are uniquely doomed; it is that everyone is, apart from God. The impossible needle is threaded only by the God for whom all things are possible.

visualMeditations.title: The Man Who Walked Away
visualMeditations.image: He came almost running — Mark tells us he ran and fell on his knees. Young, wealthy, respected, morally clean, and hungry for more. He asks the best question a man can ask. And then the King names his one idol, and the light goes out of his eyes. He rises slowly. He turns. And the last image is his back, walking away down the road, shoulders bent under invisible gold, sad.
visualMeditations.meaning: This is the only person in the Gospels who comes to Jesus sincerely and leaves worse than he came — because he would not let go. His possessions were not in his hands; they were in his heart. The tragedy is not that Jesus asked too much. The tragedy is that the man valued his money more than the treasure standing right in front of him, offering to be followed.

structure.label: The Question of Divorce (v. 1-9)
structure.body: The Pharisees test Jesus on divorce; He answers from creation, not concession — God's original one-flesh design stands above Moses' permission.

structure.label: Marriage and Singleness (v. 10-12)
structure.body: The disciples recoil at marriage's permanence; Jesus honors both the high calling of marriage and voluntary celibacy for the Kingdom's sake.

structure.label: Blessing the Little Children (v. 13-15)
structure.body: Jesus overrules His disciples and welcomes the children, declaring the Kingdom belongs to the small and dependent.

structure.label: The Rich Young Ruler (v. 16-22)
structure.body: A moral, wealthy seeker asks how to earn eternal life; Jesus exposes the idol of his riches, and he goes away sad.

structure.label: The Difficulty of Riches (v. 23-26)
structure.body: Wealth makes entering the Kingdom humanly impossible — but with God all things are possible.

structure.label: The Hundredfold Reward (v. 27-30)
structure.body: Jesus promises those who leave all for His name a hundredfold return, eternal life, and thrones — yet warns that the first will be last.

sections.heading: One Theme Under Two Roofs: The Kingdom Belongs to Those Who Receive It
paragraphs: At first glance chapter 19 looks like four unrelated scenes stitched together — divorce, children, a rich man, a reward. But a single golden thread runs through all of them, and once you see it you cannot un-see it: the Kingdom belongs to those who receive it as a gift, and it is closed to those who try to hold it (or anything) by their own strength.

The Pharisees grasp at marriage as a contract they can control and cancel; Jesus points them back to what God joined. The children grasp at nothing — and the Kingdom is theirs. The rich young ruler grasps at his wealth and his own goodness, asking what he can do, and walks away with empty hands full. The disciples let go of everything and are promised a hundredfold. The chapter is one long contrast between the clutching hand and the open hand. The clutching hand — Pharisee, ruler — goes away with nothing. The open hand — child, disciple — inherits everything.

This is why the chapter climaxes in verse 26. "With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible." That is not only about rich men and camels; it is the verdict over the whole chapter. Keeping marriage as God designed it, becoming small as a child, prying your fingers off your possessions, leaving everything to follow — none of it is within human power. All of it is possible only by the God who welds, who lifts children, who threads camels through needles, and who repays a hundredfold.

sections.heading: The Honest Difficulty: Did Jesus Really Forbid All Divorce?
paragraphs: We must not soften this text. Jesus deliberately raises the standard of marriage far above the culture around Him — and far above much of the church today. He grounds it not in Moses (who is a concession) but in creation (which is the design), and He says plainly that God is the one who joins a husband and wife into one flesh. That is why the disciples are so shaken they conclude it might be better not to marry at all (v. 10). If your view of marriage leaves you comfortable rather than sobered, you have not yet heard what Jesus said.

Jesus does state one exception — "except for sexual immorality" (porneia) — because that sin has itself already violated the one-flesh bond. And Paul, teaching the same Lord's mind, adds the case of an unbelieving spouse who abandons the marriage (1 Corinthians 7:15). But these are narrow gates, not the wide highway of "any reason" the Pharisees wanted. The heart of the passage is not a tidy list of when you may leave; it is a call to covenant faithfulness that reflects God's own faithfulness. The good news for anyone bruised by divorce is not that Jesus lowers His standard, but that He is the God for whom all things are possible — including forgiveness, healing, and the grace to keep covenant going forward.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: The very Genesis text Jesus quotes here — "the two shall become one flesh" (v. 5) — becomes, in the hands of the Apostle Paul, the deepest window into the gospel itself. In Ephesians 5:31-32 Paul cites the identical verse and then writes: "This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and of the assembly." Marriage, Paul reveals, was never merely about a husband and wife. From the beginning it was a living icon of Christ and His church — the Bridegroom who leaves His Father's glory, cleaves to His bride, and joins Himself to her so completely that they become one. That is why Jesus guards the one-flesh union so fiercely: to tear apart a marriage is to vandalize the picture God painted of His own covenant love.

And this same Jesus, whose divorce teaching Paul treats as the authoritative command of the Lord ("not I, but the Lord" — 1 Corinthians 7:10), is the One who makes the impossible possible. The rich young ruler could not save himself, and neither can you. But "with God all things are possible" (v. 26) reaches its fulfillment at the cross and empty tomb, where God did the humanly impossible — threading condemned sinners through the needle's eye of His justice by the blood of His Son. The hundredfold reward Jesus promises in verse 29 finds its guarantee in the resurrection: the King who will "sit on the throne of his glory" (v. 28) has already been raised, and John sees that very throne and hears Him say, "Behold, I am making all things new" (Revelation 21:5) — the regeneration Jesus named.

lexicon.insight: Literally "to yoke together" — from syn (together) and the root of the word for a team of oxen bound under one yoke. Marriage is not two animals walking side by side; it is two harnessed under a single yoke, made to pull as one. And the yoking is God's own act. When Jesus adds "let no man tear apart," He is saying: do not unyoke what the divine Farmer has yoked. This one word carries the whole weight of His argument.

A compound of sklēros (hard, dried out, stubborn) and kardia (heart). It pictures a heart gone stiff and calloused, like sun-baked clay. Jesus diagnoses divorce not as a right God granted but as a splint God allowed for a broken bone — Moses' concession existed only because of sklērokardia. The problem was never God's law; it was the hardened human heart. This word quietly indicts every one of us: our need for concessions is the measure of our hardness.

Not "flawless" but "complete, whole, having reached its intended end (telos)." The rich young ruler is missing the one thing that would make him whole — and it is not another rule to keep but a Person to follow. Jesus' "if you want to be perfect" is not a call to moral perfectionism; it is a call to wholeness that only comes by letting go of the false treasure and taking hold of the true. The man wanted to add eternal life to his portfolio; Jesus asked him to trade the portfolio for Himself.

Adynatos is the alpha-negative of dynatos (able, powerful — the root of "dynamite"): literally "without power, unable." Jesus places the two words face to face: with men, adynatos; with God, all things are dynatos. This is the hinge of the gospel. Salvation is not difficult-but-doable; it is flatly beyond human power. The good news is not that God helps those who help themselves, but that God does what men cannot do at all. The needle is threaded only from heaven's side.

From palin (again) and genesis (birth) — literally "the birth again" of all things. It appears only twice in the New Testament: here for the cosmic renewal when the Son of Man reigns, and in Titus 3:5 for the personal renewal of the believer ("the washing of regeneration"). The two are one story. The same power that will make the whole creation new is the power already making you new. When Jesus answers Peter's "what will we have?", He lifts his eyes to the day the universe is reborn under its rightful King.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with your grip — what your hands are clutching that is quietly keeping you out of the fullness of the Kingdom.

items.title: What Have You Torn Apart That God Joined?
items.body: Jesus says God is the one who joins, and no man should tear apart. This starts with marriage — but the Spirit widens it. What has God joined in your life that you have been prying apart with your own hands? A covenant you are quietly quitting on. A commitment you are looking for a loophole out of, the way the Pharisees hunted for "any reason." Have you been treating something God welded as though it were something you could unclip? The Spirit asks: where are you living by concession and hardness of heart instead of by God's original, beautiful design? What would it look like to stop searching for the exit and start honoring the yoke?

items.title: Have You Become Small Enough to Enter?
items.body: The disciples pushed the children away because children could not add anything to the Kingdom's importance. And that is exactly the point you keep missing. You are still trying to enter as an adult — accomplished, competent, self-sufficient, with your resume of kept commandments like the rich young ruler. But the Kingdom belongs to "ones like these": the small, the dependent, the empty-handed who receive everything as gift. The gate is low. You cannot walk through it standing tall on your achievements. Are you willing to become small? To come to Jesus with nothing in your hands, needing to be lifted like a child — or does your pride still insist on walking in on its own two feet?

items.title: Name Your One Thing
items.body: The rich young ruler kept every rule and still walked away, because there was one thing he loved more than Jesus. Here is the terrifying mercy of this chapter: Jesus loved him enough to name it. He will do the same for you. What is your "one thing" — the possession, relationship, ambition, or security that you would walk away sad rather than surrender? Do not answer quickly. The ruler did not know his god was money until Jesus asked for it. So let the Spirit ask you now: if Jesus said "go, sell that, and come, follow me," what would He point at? And would you go away sad — or would you finally be free?

audit.title: The Loophole Check
audit.body: Where in your life are you behaving like the Pharisees — searching Scripture not to obey it but to find permission to do what you have already decided to do? What covenant or commitment are you quietly looking for an escape hatch from, and what would it mean to close the escape hatch and honor what God joined?

audit.title: The 'One Thing' Audit
audit.body: If Jesus looked you in the eye today and said, "You lack one thing — go, sell it, and follow me," what is the one thing He would name? Be brutally specific. Is it money, a title, a relationship, control, your reputation, your comfort? Would you walk away sad, or hand it over?

audit.title: The Scoreboard Test
audit.body: "Many who are first will be last." Whose scoreboard are you living for? Measure your last week honestly: were your energy and joy spent chasing what makes you "first" in the eyes of people, or what makes you rich toward God? Where are you counting on being first that Jesus might call last?

practices.title: Surrender the One Thing (Do It This Week)
practices.body: This week, take the one thing the Spirit named in the audit above and put it, out loud, on the altar. Kneel down and physically hold out your open hands and say, "Lord, I give You ___. It is Yours, not mine. I unclench my fist." Then do one concrete act that proves it — give away a sum that actually costs you, forgive the person you have been holding hostage, book the conversation you have been avoiding. Turn the surrender from a feeling into an action before the week ends.

practices.title: Come as a Child (Do It Tonight)
practices.body: Tonight, come to God with nothing in your hands — no bargaining, no list of good things you have done, no "what will I get?" Take ten minutes and pray only as a small child would: "Father, I cannot do this. It is impossible for me. I am not bringing You my achievements; I am bringing You my need. Lift me." Write down one impossibility in your life and hand it over with the words of verse 26: "With men this is impossible, but with You all things are possible."

prayerReflection: "Lord Jesus, King of the low gate — I come to You today with my hands open. I confess how often I have lived like the Pharisees, hunting for loopholes instead of honoring what You joined; how often I have lived like the rich young ruler, sincere and moral and still clutching my one thing more tightly than I clutch You. Forgive my hardness of heart. Make me small again. Give me the child's empty hands that receive everything as gift, for I know that the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to ones like these. Show me the one thing I love more than You, and give me the grace not to walk away sad but to lay it down and follow. I believe that what is impossible for me is possible for You — so do in me what I cannot do in myself. Weld my heart to Yours. And I trust Your promise: that everything surrendered for Your name's sake is not lost but exchanged, a hundredfold now and eternal life to come. I let go, Lord. I follow. In Jesus' name, Amen."

storyConnections.title: The First Marriage in the Garden
storyConnections.summary: When Jesus is asked about divorce, He does not go to the courtroom of Moses; He goes back to the wedding in Eden. There God saw that it was not good for the man to be alone, put Adam into a deep sleep, took a rib, and built a woman. Adam's first recorded poetry was over his bride: "bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh." Then comes the line Jesus quotes: "Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall join with his wife, and they will be one flesh." Jesus is telling the Pharisees that marriage is older than the Law, woven into creation itself — which is why no human court can simply un-weave it.

storyConnections.title: Elisha Leaves the Plow to Follow
storyConnections.summary: Where the rich young ruler could not leave his possessions, Elisha shows the opposite response. When Elijah threw his mantle over him, Elisha was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen — a sign of real wealth. He slaughtered his oxen, burned his plowing equipment to cook the meat, fed the people, and left everything to follow the prophet. He literally destroyed his means of turning back. Elisha is the living picture of "come, follow me," and of the disciples who "left everything and followed" — and God gave him a double portion, a hundredfold return on what he surrendered.

storyConnections.title: Zacchaeus: The Rich Man Who Let Go
storyConnections.summary: If chapter 19 leaves you wondering whether any rich man can be saved, Luke gives the answer just a few chapters later. Zacchaeus was a wealthy chief tax collector — exactly the kind of man for whom entering the Kingdom was "impossible." Yet when Jesus called him down from the sycamore tree and came to his house, Zacchaeus stood up and said, "Behold, half of my goods I give to the poor, and if I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much." The camel went through the needle's eye. Jesus declared, "Today, salvation has come to this house." What was impossible with men proved gloriously possible with God.
